title: Profit Center × Equipment-Centric
summary: Service is a margin line earned on an installed base, and margin starts with control of the work. Every request lands in one queue, every job has an owner and a visible status, and every technician arrives with the machine's history. Pricing, parts, warranty, and agreements build on that backbone in phase two.

tiers.label: Tier 1: Go-live
tiers.description: The intake, scheduling, and dispatch backbone. Nothing downstream is reliable without it.

tiers.label: Tier 2: Phase two
tiers.description: Parts, pricing, warranty, and agreements, once the job data coming out of Tier 1 can be trusted.

tiers.label: Tier 3: Later or optional
tiers.description: Optimization and connected equipment, once there is enough real history to tune them.

jobs.title: Turn every qualified request into one work order
jobs.detail: Requests from phone, email, and portal become a work order with the minimum data a dispatcher needs: service address, contact, work type, and the machine.

jobs.title: Put all unscheduled work in one queue
jobs.detail: One queue across every intake channel, with aging and urgent work surfaced first, prioritized by the customer commitment behind each job.

jobs.title: Make every assignment visible and owned
jobs.detail: A shared board replaces trust-based assignment: everyone can see who owns a job, when it is booked, and where it stands.

jobs.title: Schedule by territory, hours, and travel
jobs.detail: Technicians route from their home base within working hours. Territory guides the choice without blocking dispatch from covering a staffing gap.

jobs.title: Tie every job to the customer's machine
jobs.detail: Each work order points to a customer asset, and a new installation cannot close until the machine is identified.

jobs.title: Give technicians a simple mobile day
jobs.detail: Route, job details, customer and branch context, and the machine's prior service history on one screen, before the truck leaves.

jobs.title: Track status through the job, including holds
jobs.detail: Technicians update status as they travel, work, and finish. Work waiting on parts, approval, or the customer shows a reason instead of disappearing.

jobs.title: Capture structured findings and keep follow-up work open
jobs.detail: Complaint, cause, and correction are recorded in fields, not one free-text note. A diagnostic visit closes its booking while the work order stays open for the return trip.

jobs.title: Review completed work before it posts
jobs.detail: A manager checks every completed job before it moves to billing, so errors are fixed once instead of chased later.

jobs.title: Record parts and labor, then manage truck stock
jobs.detail: Parts used are captured on the job and drawn down from the truck, so they are either covered or billed.

jobs.title: Price from price lists and customer agreements
jobs.detail: Labor, parts, and travel charges come from the agreed price list for that customer and region, not from technician judgment.

jobs.title: Show warranty and coverage on the machine
jobs.detail: Dispatch and technicians see whether the machine is under warranty or contract before the visit, drawn from the system of record.

jobs.title: Generate planned maintenance from service agreements
jobs.detail: Recurring inspections and maintenance come from the agreement, not from each branch remembering.

jobs.title: Optimize schedules automatically
jobs.detail: Automated scheduling and long-distance routing, once job durations, territories, and skills reflect real history.

jobs.title: Create jobs from connected-equipment alerts
jobs.detail: Machine telemetry opens a case before the customer notices a fault. A step toward the Servitizing row.

kpis.name: Time from request to booking
kpis.definition: Elapsed time from a qualified request to a confirmed booking with a technician.
kpis.whyItMatters: It is the first thing the customer feels, and the first place a decentralized intake process shows up.
kpis.whatGoodLooksLike: Falling and consistent across channels, with urgent work booked first.

kpis.name: Promise-window adherence
kpis.definition: Share of visits where the technician arrived inside the window promised to the customer.
kpis.whyItMatters: Customer commitments only mean something if they drive scheduling. This tests whether they do.
kpis.whatGoodLooksLike: Rising, with every miss traced to scheduling, travel, or an overrun earlier in the day.

kpis.name: First-time fix rate
kpis.definition: Share of jobs resolved on the first visit with no return trip for the same fault.
kpis.whyItMatters: Every return trip is labor the customer rarely pays for twice. It is the clearest test of whether history and parts reach the technician.
kpis.whatGoodLooksLike: Rising quarter over quarter, with return visits traced to a named cause.

kpis.name: Daily carryover rate
kpis.definition: Share of booked work that ends the day unfinished and has to be rebooked.
kpis.whyItMatters: Carryover exposes weak duration estimates and hidden holds before they turn into missed commitments.
kpis.whatGoodLooksLike: Falling, with each carried-over job showing a hold reason.

kpis.name: Technician utilization
kpis.definition: Share of paid technician hours spent on productive work rather than travel, waiting, or admin.
kpis.whyItMatters: Labor is the largest cost in the service margin. Better routing and less re-keying show up here first.
kpis.whatGoodLooksLike: Rising without first-time fix falling, which would signal rushed work.

kpis.name: Complete-at-close rate
kpis.definition: Share of completed jobs that close with every required field: asset, findings, parts, labor, and sign-off.
kpis.whyItMatters: Billing, warranty, and asset history all depend on what the technician records at close.
kpis.whatGoodLooksLike: Near complete, so review is a check rather than a rebuild.

kpis.name: Days from completion to invoice
kpis.definition: Elapsed time between a job being completed and the invoice being issued.
kpis.whyItMatters: Slow invoicing delays cash and invites disputes because the visit is no longer fresh for the customer.
kpis.whatGoodLooksLike: Falling toward the target the client sets in discovery, and consistent across branches.

kpis.name: Service gross margin
kpis.definition: Service revenue less the direct cost of labor, parts, and travel, as a share of service revenue.
kpis.whyItMatters: This is the number service leadership wants to be judged on. The other KPIs explain why it moves.
kpis.whatGoodLooksLike: Reported by branch and service line from the system, not assembled in a spreadsheet.

questionSet.question: How many different ways does a service request reach you today, and which one should be the front door?
questionSet.whyWeAsk: Decentralized intake is the most common blocker to a single scheduling queue. We need to know every channel before we design one.
questionSet.goodAnswer: A short list of channels, a named owner for each, and agreement that every request ends up as a work order in one place.

redFlags.answer: "It depends on the branch, and some of it comes in by text to the technician."
redFlags.signals: Work is invisible until someone re-keys it. Expect a Phase 1 intake decision before scheduling design can finish.

redFlags.answer: "We'd like every channel integrated on day one."
redFlags.signals: Likely off-blueprint request. Start with manual intake into one queue and integrate once the intake fields are stable.

questionSet.question: What is the minimum a request needs before someone can schedule it?
questionSet.whyWeAsk: It sets the required fields on the work order and the mapping from every intake channel.
questionSet.goodAnswer: Address, contact phone, work type, customer, and the machine, agreed once and enforced at creation.

redFlags.answer: "Whatever the caller gives us; the tech sorts it out."
redFlags.signals: Jobs will be scheduled without the data to finish them. Expect return trips and calls from the field.

redFlags.answer: "Every customer needs something different."
redFlags.signals: Customer-specific fields multiply fast. Separate the true minimum from account instructions.

questionSet.question: When a request comes in, how do you know whether the machine is under warranty or a service contract?
questionSet.whyWeAsk: Coverage decides who pays. If it is invisible at intake, it is decided on site, inconsistently.
questionSet.goodAnswer: Warranty and contract status are visible on the machine record before the visit, from one system of record.

redFlags.answer: "The tech checks the other system when they get there."
redFlags.signals: Coverage lives outside the service record. Plan a warranty-visibility decision and a later integration.

redFlags.answer: "We don't track which individual machines are covered."
redFlags.signals: Asset-level entitlement needs its own discovery. Keep it out of go-live scope.

questionSet.question: Once a job is assigned, how does everyone know who owns it and where it stands?
questionSet.whyWeAsk: Trust-based assignment works until volume grows. Visible ownership is a Tier 1 job.
questionSet.goodAnswer: Every booking has one owner and a current status that dispatch and the branch can both see.

redFlags.answer: "We call the tech and ask."
redFlags.signals: No shared status. Booking status and hold reasons need to be defined early.

redFlags.answer: "The technician knows, and they're good about it."
redFlags.signals: Ownership lives with people. Expect resistance to status updates until the benefit is shown.

questionSet.question: Should a technician's territory limit which jobs they can take, or only guide the choice?
questionSet.whyWeAsk: Territories that act as hard walls break staffing-gap coverage. This decides how scheduling rules are built.
questionSet.goodAnswer: Territory is a preference. Dispatch can send someone across a boundary when that is the better answer.

redFlags.answer: "Techs should only ever see their own area."
redFlags.signals: Likely off-blueprint request for a hard territory rule. Ask how often jobs already cross boundaries.

redFlags.answer: "We haven't agreed where the boundaries are."
redFlags.signals: Territory design is a go-live blocker. Get the geographic structure decided first.

questionSet.question: What should happen when a booking would push a technician into overtime?
questionSet.whyWeAsk: Overtime policy drives the scheduling guardrail: a warning, an approval, or a hard stop.
questionSet.goodAnswer: A warning first, with a named approver for exceptions, and the rule written down.

redFlags.answer: "It should never be allowed."
redFlags.signals: A hard stop blocks emergency work. Test it against real emergency scenarios before building it.

redFlags.answer: "The branch manager decides case by case."
redFlags.signals: No policy yet. The guardrail cannot be configured until there is one.

questionSet.question: What does a technician record today about the parts and labor on a job, and who uses it?
questionSet.whyWeAsk: It sets the minimum work detail for go-live and shows whether full parts capture belongs in phase two.
questionSet.goodAnswer: A short, agreed list of what is captured on every job, and a named consumer for each item.

redFlags.answer: "They write it on the paper ticket and billing figures it out."
redFlags.signals: Parts are invisible to billing. Unbilled work is likely high.

redFlags.answer: "We need full truck inventory at go-live."
redFlags.signals: Full inventory is a phase-two scope. Ask what decision it enables at go-live.

questionSet.question: Do you ever send a technician to diagnose a problem before the parts are confirmed?
questionSet.whyWeAsk: Parts availability as a hard stop blocks diagnostic visits. This decides how the follow-up visit works.
questionSet.goodAnswer: Yes. The diagnostic visit is scheduled, parts are identified on site, and a follow-up booking is created from the same work order.

redFlags.answer: "We wait until the parts are in before we go."
redFlags.signals: Customers wait longer than they need to. Check whether the delay is policy or habit.

questionSet.question: Who knows what is on each truck right now?
questionSet.whyWeAsk: Truck stock accuracy decides whether parts capture can drive replenishment later.
questionSet.goodAnswer: A named role owns stock levels per truck, and counts are trusted enough to act on.

redFlags.answer: "Each tech manages their own truck."
redFlags.signals: No inventory accountability. Stock data will need a clean-up before phase two.

questionSet.question: What does a technician need on the phone before they drive to a job?
questionSet.whyWeAsk: The mobile screen should carry the minimum, not everything. Too much on it slows adoption.
questionSet.goodAnswer: Address and route, contact, work type, the machine and its history, and any customer instructions.

redFlags.answer: "Everything we have today, plus a few more fields."
redFlags.signals: Mobile scope creep. Ask which fields are used on every job.

redFlags.answer: "They don't really use the tablet."
redFlags.signals: Adoption risk. Plan a hands-on mobile walkthrough before design sign-off.

questionSet.question: When a job cannot be finished, what reasons do you actually see?
questionSet.whyWeAsk: Hold reasons turn "still open" into something dispatch can act on.
questionSet.goodAnswer: A short list of real reasons, such as waiting on parts, customer, or approval, each with a next step.

redFlags.answer: "It just stays open until someone notices."
redFlags.signals: Stalled work is invisible. Carryover and missed commitments are likely higher than anyone thinks.

questionSet.question: Can a technician decline a job that dispatch has assigned?
questionSet.whyWeAsk: It decides how bookings are confirmed and who holds the schedule.
questionSet.goodAnswer: No, but a technician can flag a problem and dispatch reassigns, with the reason recorded.

redFlags.answer: "Yes, they turn down what they don't want."
redFlags.signals: Dispatch does not control the schedule. Expect a governance conversation before configuration.

questionSet.question: Who reviews completed work before it is billed, and what do they usually fix?
questionSet.whyWeAsk: The review step is a Tier 1 control. What reviewers fix shows which close rules are missing.
questionSet.goodAnswer: A named reviewer checks every job at first, and the most common corrections become required fields.

redFlags.answer: "Billing fixes it when the customer complains."
redFlags.signals: Errors reach the invoice. Complete-at-close is likely low.

questionSet.question: Should technicians be able to change prices or costs on a job?
questionSet.whyWeAsk: Pricing authority in the field varies margin by who shows up.
questionSet.goodAnswer: Prices come from the price list. Technicians flag exceptions, and a manager approves them.

redFlags.answer: "They need to, because the price list is never right."
redFlags.signals: The price list is the real problem. Fix it rather than opening every price to change.

redFlags.answer: "Each tech has their own rates for certain customers."
redFlags.signals: Likely request for custom pricing rules. Ask what business rule it really serves.

questionSet.question: How is service priced when the same customer buys in different regions?
questionSet.whyWeAsk: Customer and regional pricing decides the price-list model, and it is often unresolved at kickoff.
questionSet.goodAnswer: One pricing hierarchy, written down, with the drivers named: customer tier, region, and work type.

redFlags.answer: "It varies; the account manager knows."
redFlags.signals: Pricing is undefined. Keep it in phase two and name an owner for the decision.

redFlags.answer: "Every customer has its own mileage and travel rules."
redFlags.signals: Travel-charge automation is a phase-two candidate. Start with standard charges.

questionSet.question: What is the minimum you need to know about a customer's machine?
questionSet.whyWeAsk: It sets the required asset fields and how much data work sits in front of go-live.
questionSet.goodAnswer: Make, model, serial number, and location for every machine, captured at installation.

redFlags.answer: "Between the ERP, the warranty system, and the branches, we could piece it together."
redFlags.signals: The installed base needs consolidation. Plan data work, not just configuration.

questionSet.question: When a machine leaves the customer site for repair, how do you track it?
questionSet.whyWeAsk: Off-site custody is a common gap. Without it, history and accountability break.
questionSet.goodAnswer: The machine's location and custody change are recorded, so anyone can see where it is.

redFlags.answer: "We just know which shop it went to."
redFlags.signals: No custody process. Treat it as a later-phase design item.

questionSet.question: How far back can a technician see this machine's service history today?
questionSet.whyWeAsk: History on site is the fastest route to first-time fix.
questionSet.goodAnswer: Every prior visit on this machine, whoever performed it, visible on mobile.

redFlags.answer: "Only their own jobs."
redFlags.signals: History is siloed by technician. Visibility and security need to be designed together.

redFlags.answer: "It's in the other system."
redFlags.signals: Split system of record. Decide which system owns the technician's work before go-live.

process.label: Aligned to vendor standard process catalogs.
process.note: Platform-agnostic. Each step lists the control the blueprint puts in place.

steps.name: Request and qualify
steps.description: A request from any channel becomes a work order with the minimum data.
steps.guardrail: Required intake fields enforced at creation.

steps.name: Entitlement check
steps.description: Warranty and contract coverage checked against the machine.
steps.guardrail: Covered versus billable decided before scheduling.

steps.name: Schedule
steps.description: Booked from one queue by priority, territory, hours, and travel.
steps.guardrail: Urgent and aging work surfaced first.

steps.name: Dispatch
steps.description: The booking reaches the technician's mobile day.
steps.guardrail: One owner and a visible status for every job.

steps.name: Execute
steps.description: The technician diagnoses and repairs on site.
steps.guardrail: Hold reasons recorded when work cannot finish.

steps.name: Parts
steps.description: Parts used are recorded against the job.

steps.name: Complete
steps.description: Findings, asset identity, and sign-off captured; follow-up work stays open.
steps.guardrail: Job cannot close with required fields missing.

steps.name: Review and invoice
steps.description: A manager reviews the job, then billable work is priced and invoiced.

steps.name: Asset-history update
steps.description: Findings and parts written back to the machine's record.
steps.guardrail: The next technician starts with the full history.
